lesson.title: Cesar Chavez, Dolores Huerta, and the Rise of the United Farm Workers
lesson.summary: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta built a farmworkers' union out of one of the poorest and most powerless workforces in America, and the Delano grape strike and boycott they led turned a local labor dispute into a national civil rights cause.
lesson.body:
Farmworkers in California's Central Valley in the early 1960s, many of them Mexican American or Filipino American, worked long hours for low wages with no job security and little legal protection, since federal labor law had specifically excluded agricultural workers from the right to unionize. In 1962, Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta founded the National Farm Workers Association in the Delano, California area, aiming to organize these workers into a union that could bargain for better wages and conditions. Chavez had grown up in a family of migrant farmworkers and had worked as a community organizer, while Huerta brought experience in political organizing and became one of the union's most effective negotiators and strategists.

The turning point came in September 1965. Filipino American grape pickers belonging to the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee, led by Larry Itliong, went on strike against Delano area grape growers on September 8, 1965, demanding wages equal to the federal minimum wage. Chavez's organization voted to join the strike on September 16, 1965, and the two groups merged the following year to form the United Farm Workers, which affiliated with the AFL-CIO, the same federation of unions that traced its organizing traditions back to the American Federation of Labor. The merger combined Filipino and Mexican American farmworkers into a single union at a time when growers had long used ethnic divisions among workers to prevent organizing.

The Delano grape strike stretched on for years, and Chavez and Huerta expanded it into a national grape boycott, asking American consumers to stop buying table grapes until growers agreed to union contracts. The UFW organized boycott committees in cities across the country and drew support from clergy, students, and other labor unions. Chavez, deeply influenced by the nonviolent philosophy of Mohandas Gandhi and by Martin Luther King Jr., insisted on nonviolent tactics even as strikers faced violence from growers and local authorities, and in 1968 he undertook a 25 day fast to recommit the movement to nonviolence.

The pressure worked. By 1970, most of the major Delano area grape growers had signed contracts recognizing the United Farm Workers and raising wages. The victory made Chavez one of the most recognized labor leaders in the country and established the UFW as a lasting institution, though the union continued to fight grower resistance and internal challenges for years afterward. The farmworkers' movement also became closely tied to the broader push for Mexican American civil rights in the 1960s and 1970s, sometimes called the Chicano movement, showing how the era's civil rights energy, first mobilized nationally around the Civil Rights Act of 1964, extended beyond questions of race into questions of labor and economic justice.
